title: Asthma: Confirm Variable Airflow Disease, Then Step Treatment to Control
bottomLine: Asthma is a variable-airflow disease diagnosed from a compatible symptom pattern plus objective evidence when feasible. Management is anchored in inhaled corticosteroid-containing therapy, technique/adherence and trigger/comorbidity review, with escalation based on control and exacerbation risk rather than symptoms alone.
recognize: Episodic wheeze, cough, chest tightness and dyspnea that vary over time or with triggers support asthma.
Normal spirometry between episodes does not exclude asthma when the clinical pattern remains convincing.
differentiate: COPD, inducible laryngeal obstruction, heart failure, eosinophilic bronchitis and anxiety can mimic asthma.
Poor control may reflect wrong diagnosis, poor technique/adherence, ongoing exposure or comorbidity rather than inadequate drug intensity.
assessment: Assess symptom frequency, nighttime waking, activity limitation, exacerbations, reliever use, smoking/vaping, occupation, rhinitis/reflux, adherence and inhaler technique.
workup: Use spirometry with bronchodilator response when feasible and additional variability testing when uncertainty remains.
Do not order broad imaging or eosinophil panels routinely unless the phenotype/severity warrants them.
management: Use current CTS stepwise asthma therapy with ICS-containing treatment and step up or down after confirming diagnosis, technique, adherence and triggers.
Provide a written action plan and escalate severe exacerbation or life-threatening features urgently.
medicationSafety: Repeated oral corticosteroid bursts are a signal to reassess control and specialist referral because cumulative toxicity is important.
redFlags: Poor response to initial bronchodilator therapy
counselling: Teach spacer/device technique, action-plan zones, trigger reduction and when to seek urgent care.
followUp: Reassess control, exacerbations, technique and adherence after changes; step down only after sustained control and individualized review.
examTrap: Escalating medication without first checking whether the diagnosis, inhaler technique and adherence are correct.
oneLinePearl: Asthma treatment starts with confirming variable disease and always checking technique before adding more therapy.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society current asthma guideline and focused update

title: COPD: Confirm Persistent Obstruction and Treat Symptoms plus Exacerbation Risk
bottomLine: COPD requires persistent airflow obstruction in the correct exposure and clinical context. Management combines smoking/exposure treatment, vaccination, inhaled therapy, pulmonary rehabilitation and exacerbation prevention matched to symptom and risk burden—not a drug decision based on FEV1 alone.
recognize: Progressive exertional dyspnea, chronic cough/sputum and exposure history support COPD.
Exacerbation is an acute worsening beyond usual day-to-day variation and should prompt evaluation for pneumonia, heart failure, PE and other mimics.
differentiate: Asthma has variable airflow disease and may coexist with COPD; a history of smoking does not prove COPD.
Heart failure, ILD and deconditioning can cause disproportionate dyspnea with similar symptoms.
assessment: Assess smoking/vaping/occupational exposure, symptom burden, exacerbation/hospital history, oxygenation, inhaler technique, comorbidity, weight and functional status.
workup: Confirm persistent obstruction with quality spirometry after bronchodilator according to the current CTS diagnostic approach.
Use imaging, alpha-1 antitrypsin testing or additional studies when age, severity or phenotype makes them clinically appropriate.
management: Use current CTS stable-COPD pharmacotherapy based on symptoms/exacerbations and individual response, plus smoking cessation, vaccination and rehabilitation.
Exacerbations with severe dyspnea, hypoxemia, acidosis, confusion or inability to cope require acute-care escalation.
medicationSafety: ICS is not universally indicated in COPD; weigh exacerbation phenotype against pneumonia and other risks.
Avoid chronic oral corticosteroids for stable COPD.
counselling: Teach inhaler technique, action planning, smoking cessation and pulmonary-rehabilitation value.
followUp: Track symptoms, exacerbations, adherence/technique and functional status; repeat spirometry when it answers a clinical question rather than on autopilot.
examTrap: Calling COPD from symptoms alone without spirometric confirmation—or adding ICS automatically to every obstructed smoker.
oneLinePearl: COPD is confirmed by persistent obstruction; treatment is driven by symptoms and exacerbations, not FEV1 alone.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society 2023 COPD pharmacotherapy guideline and current COPD tools

title: Pneumonia: Community or Healthcare Exposure Changes the Empiric Plan
bottomLine: Pneumonia treatment starts with severity and setting. Confirm a compatible lower-respiratory syndrome, distinguish community-onset from hospital/healthcare-associated risk patterns, choose empiric therapy using current local guidance and resistance risk, then narrow or stop when data change the diagnosis.
recognize: Fever, cough, sputum, dyspnea, pleuritic pain, focal lung findings and a new infiltrate support pneumonia; older adults may present with delirium or functional decline.
Recent hospitalization, ventilation or resistant-organism history changes empiric risk assessment.
differentiate: Acute bronchitis usually lacks a new pneumonia infiltrate and does not justify antibiotics in a stable patient.
PE, heart failure, aspiration pneumonitis and viral infection can mimic pneumonia.
assessment: Assess oxygenation, hemodynamics, confusion, oral intake, aspiration risk, comorbidity, recent antibiotics/hospitalization and prior resistant organisms.
workup: Use chest imaging when pneumonia diagnosis/disposition requires confirmation and obtain cultures in severe disease or when resistance data will change therapy.
Do not order sputum cultures routinely in uncomplicated ambulatory pneumonia when they will not change management.
management: Use current Canadian/local empiric regimens matched to setting, severity and resistance risk, with reassessment and de-escalation.
Admit or escalate when oxygenation, hemodynamics, mental status, oral intake or social safety makes outpatient care unsafe.
medicationSafety: Check allergies, renal/hepatic function, QT risk, drug interactions and C. difficile risk.
Avoid unnecessarily prolonged courses when uncomplicated disease is improving.
counselling: Explain expected recovery, antibiotic adherence when indicated and specific return precautions for worsening dyspnea, confusion, fever or poor intake.
followUp: Reassess clinically when expected improvement does not occur and reconsider diagnosis, resistance or complication rather than automatically broadening antibiotics.
examTrap: Treating every cough with an antibiotic—or choosing the same empiric regimen despite recent hospitalization and resistant-organism risk.
oneLinePearl: For pneumonia, severity and exposure history shape both disposition and empiric therapy.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Cold Standard respiratory stewardship
Canadian antimicrobial stewardship and acute-care pneumonia pathways

title: Pulmonary Embolism: Pretest Probability Before D-Dimer, Stability Before Disposition
bottomLine: PE evaluation is probability-driven. Estimate pretest probability first, use D-dimer only when it can safely exclude disease, obtain definitive imaging when indicated, and separate hemodynamically unstable/high-risk PE from stable patients who may be candidates for anticoagulation and selected outpatient care.
recognize: Unexplained dyspnea, pleuritic pain, tachycardia, hypoxemia, hemoptysis or syncope can occur; presentation can be subtle.
Recent surgery/immobility, active cancer, estrogen/pregnancy, prior VTE and thrombophilia raise risk.
differentiate: D-dimer is a rule-out test in selected low/intermediate-probability patients, not a diagnostic test for PE.
Pneumonia, ACS, pneumothorax, heart failure and panic can mimic PE.
assessment: Assess hemodynamics, oxygenation, bleeding risk, VTE risk factors, DVT symptoms, pregnancy and contraindications to anticoagulation/thrombolysis.
workup: Use a validated probability pathway with D-dimer or imaging as appropriate; pregnancy requires a pregnancy-adapted diagnostic approach.
Assess RV strain and biomarkers when they will change risk classification/disposition.
management: Start anticoagulation when indicated and safe once the diagnostic/risk pathway supports it; unstable PE requires emergency reperfusion/critical-care management.
Selected stable low-risk patients may be managed outpatient only when bleeding risk, comorbidity, access and follow-up are appropriate.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulant choice depends on renal function, pregnancy, cancer context, interactions and bleeding risk.
Do not use thrombolysis routinely in stable low-risk PE.
counselling: Teach anticoagulant adherence, bleeding precautions, recurrence symptoms and when emergency reassessment is needed.
followUp: Define treatment duration and reassess provoking factors, recurrence/bleeding and persistent dyspnea that could signal chronic thromboembolic disease.
examTrap: Ordering a D-dimer in a patient whose pretest probability is already high—or calling a positive D-dimer PE without imaging.
oneLinePearl: Probability chooses the PE test; stability chooses the disposition.
sourceBasis: Thrombosis Canada pulmonary embolism clinical guides

title: Obstructive Sleep Apnea: Diagnose Sleep-Disordered Breathing, Then Treat the Risk
bottomLine: OSA diagnosis requires a compatible clinical picture plus sleep testing when indicated; snoring alone is not OSA. Treatment depends on severity, symptoms, cardiometabolic risk, anatomy and patient preference, with PAP therapy requiring adherence/efficacy follow-up rather than a one-time prescription.
recognize: Loud snoring, witnessed apneas, choking/gasping, unrefreshing sleep, daytime sleepiness and resistant hypertension raise concern.
Sleepiness is not always present; insomnia, nocturia, headache or cognitive complaints can be part of the presentation.
differentiate: Central sleep apnea, insomnia, restless legs, narcolepsy, circadian disorders and insufficient sleep require different pathways.
Obesity increases risk but OSA occurs across body sizes.
assessment: Assess sleep schedule, witnessed events, sleepiness-related driving/work risk, sedatives/alcohol, cardiovascular disease, craniofacial/nasal factors and comorbid lung/neuromuscular disease.
workup: Use home sleep apnea testing or polysomnography according to pretest probability and comorbidity; complex cardiopulmonary/neuromuscular disease may require lab-based testing.
Do not diagnose severity from a screening questionnaire alone.
management: Use PAP for appropriate symptomatic or clinically significant OSA, plus weight-neutral health counselling, positional/anatomic strategies or oral-appliance referral when appropriate.
Address dangerous sleepiness and driving risk explicitly.
medicationSafety: Sedatives, opioids and alcohol can worsen sleep-disordered breathing and should be reviewed.
PAP efficacy requires data/symptom review; pressure intolerance should prompt troubleshooting rather than abandonment.
counselling: Teach mask/device troubleshooting, adherence expectations, humidification and why symptom improvement and objective control both matter.
followUp: Review PAP use/leak/residual events and symptoms, and reassess alternative diagnoses when adequate PAP does not resolve impairment.
examTrap: Diagnosing OSA from snoring and a questionnaire without appropriate sleep testing—or prescribing CPAP with no adherence/efficacy follow-up.
oneLinePearl: Screening finds OSA risk; sleep testing establishes the disorder and follow-up proves treatment works.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society / Canadian Sleep Society sleep-disordered breathing resources

title: Hemoptysis: Stabilize the Airway, Then Find the Source
bottomLine: Hemoptysis severity is determined by airway/respiratory/hemodynamic threat, not an imprecise volume estimate alone. Stabilize significant bleeding first, distinguish true lower-respiratory bleeding from upper-airway or GI sources, and evaluate infection, malignancy, bronchiectasis, PE and other causes based on risk.
recognize: Blood mixed with sputum or coughed from the lower respiratory tract differs from hematemesis or posterior epistaxis.
Large ongoing bleeding can kill by airway obstruction before exsanguination.
differentiate: Common causes include infection, bronchiectasis, malignancy and inflammatory disease; PE is considered in the correct syndrome rather than assumed from hemoptysis alone.
Pseudohemoptysis from nose/oropharynx and hematemesis need different workups.
assessment: Assess airway, oxygenation, hemodynamics, bleeding trajectory, anticoagulants, infection symptoms, cancer risk, TB risk and prior lung disease.
workup: Use chest imaging and CBC/coagulation studies as clinically indicated; CT/bronchoscopy are selected based on severity, source localization and malignancy/structural concern.
management: Significant active bleeding requires emergency airway/critical-care and interventional bronchoscopy/radiology/surgery pathways.
Stable minor hemoptysis still needs cause-directed follow-up when risk factors or abnormal imaging are present.
medicationSafety: Review anticoagulants/antiplatelets and reversal needs according to bleeding severity and thrombotic risk; do not apply a universal reversal strategy.
redFlags: Known lung cancer/bronchiectasis with worsening bleed
counselling: Teach immediate emergency care for recurrent large-volume or respiratory-compromising bleeding.
followUp: Ensure diagnostic imaging/bronchoscopy and cancer/TB evaluation are completed when indicated even if bleeding stops.
examTrap: Reassuring a high-risk smoker because the hemoptysis stopped—or estimating risk solely from a guessed blood volume.
oneLinePearl: In hemoptysis, airway threat comes before etiologic elegance.
sourceBasis: Canadian respiratory and acute-care hemoptysis practice principles

title: Chronic Cough: Use a Structured Differential Before Repeating Antibiotics
bottomLine: Chronic cough requires a structured evaluation of smoking/exposures, medications, upper-airway disease, asthma/eosinophilic airway disease, reflux, infection and structural lung disease. Repeated empiric antibiotics without a bacterial syndrome delay the real diagnosis.
recognize: ACE inhibitors, smoking/vaping, rhinitis/postnasal symptoms, variable wheeze, reflux and environmental exposure are common contributors.
Red flags such as hemoptysis, weight loss, abnormal imaging, hypoxemia or immunocompromise change the urgency.
differentiate: Asthma/cough-variant asthma and eosinophilic bronchitis differ from infection; GERD symptoms can coexist without proving cough causation.
Persistent cough after viral infection can last weeks and does not automatically require antibiotics.
assessment: Clarify duration, triggers, sputum, nocturnal/exertional pattern, medications, smoking/vaping, workplace exposure, reflux/upper-airway symptoms and systemic red flags.
workup: Use chest radiograph and spirometry when clinically appropriate for chronic cough, then targeted testing based on the leading differential.
Avoid indiscriminate CT, antibiotics or reflux treatment without supporting features or failure of a structured pathway.
management: Remove obvious contributors when possible and treat the most supported cause with a defined trial and reassessment endpoint.
Refer refractory or unexplained cough, abnormal imaging or significant structural/neurologic concern to specialty care.
medicationSafety: Stop/review ACE inhibitor contribution when plausible and avoid chronic opioid antitussives without a carefully justified indication.
counselling: Set expectations that chronic cough often needs sequential testing/treatment trials rather than one immediate diagnosis.
followUp: Document response to each targeted trial so ineffective therapy is stopped and the differential is revised.
examTrap: Giving a third antibiotic course for months of cough without spirometry, medication review or chest imaging when indicated.
oneLinePearl: Chronic cough is an algorithm problem, not an antibiotic problem.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society airway disease resources

title: Tuberculosis: Test for Infection Only When the Result Changes Prevention, Diagnose Disease Microbiologically
bottomLine: TB infection testing is for people with meaningful infection/progression risk who could benefit from preventive treatment; TST/IGRA do not diagnose active TB disease in adults. Suspected pulmonary TB requires infection-control precautions, chest imaging and microbiologic testing, with public-health coordination and multidrug therapy when disease is confirmed or strongly suspected.
recognize: Cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss, hemoptysis or abnormal imaging may occur, but presentations can be subtle.
Risk is higher with close exposure, birth/residence in higher-incidence settings, immune suppression and selected congregate/occupational contexts.
differentiate: Latent TB infection has immunologic evidence without active disease; active TB requires clinical/radiologic/microbiologic assessment.
A positive TST/IGRA cannot distinguish latent from active disease and should not be used to monitor treatment response.
assessment: Assess symptoms, exposure/contact history, country/residence history, immune status, pregnancy, prior testing/treatment, medications and public-health context.
workup: Use TST or IGRA only when indicated for infection testing; suspected disease requires chest imaging plus appropriate sputum NAAT, smear/culture and drug-susceptibility testing.
Apply airborne precautions and notify public health according to jurisdiction when active pulmonary TB is suspected.
management: Treat active TB with multidrug therapy through a TB/public-health program and adjust when susceptibility data return.
Offer preventive treatment to appropriate infected patients after active disease is excluded, using current Canadian regimens and interaction monitoring.
medicationSafety: Rifamycins have major drug interactions; isoniazid/rifamycins/pyrazinamide require hepatic-risk review and monitoring based on the regimen and patient.
Pregnancy, transplant/HIV therapy and liver disease materially change regimen/interaction decisions.
counselling: Use culturally safe, non-stigmatizing counselling and explain why public-health follow-up protects both the patient and contacts.
Support adherence with the TB program rather than framing missed doses as noncompliance.
followUp: Close the loop on cultures/susceptibility, treatment toxicity, contact investigation and recurrence risk after therapy.
examTrap: Using a positive IGRA to diagnose active pulmonary TB in an adult instead of obtaining microbiologic disease testing.
oneLinePearl: TST/IGRA diagnose TB infection; active TB is a clinical-radiologic-microbiologic diagnosis.
